title: 米中露首脳会談 19日に中国で開催
body: 米ホワイトハウスは13日、トランプ大統領が中国の習近平（シーチンピン）国家主席、ロシアのプーチン大統領と19日に中国の深圳で会談すると明らかにした。米中ロ3カ国による正式な首脳会談は史上初めてとみられる。【画像】「終わりの始まり」トランプ外交　中ロ朝の指導者に操られるリスクトランプ氏は深圳で18、19両日に開かれるアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に参加する予定で、それに合わせて3カ国会談を行うとの見通しを示していた。プーチン氏も当初から前向きな姿勢を見せていた。会談での議題について、トランプ氏はこれまで核軍備管理などに言及している。ホワイトハウス高官は13日、「大統領は核兵器の拡散が極めて危険だと考えている」と説明し、世界で最も多くの核兵器を持つ3カ国首脳による最初の対話だと強調した。一方、今回の会談では「いかなる合意に至ることも予想していない」と述べ、核軍縮に向けた「出発点」と位置づけた。

title: 米でタンカーがクルーズ船に衝突
body: （CNN）　米南部ルイジアナ州のニューオーリンズ港付近で13日、タンカーがリバークルーズ船に衝突する事故があった。ニューオーリンズのモレノ市長によると、クルーズ船の乗客全員の安否が確認されており、命に関わるけがを負った人はいない。【映像】タンカーがリバークルーズ船に衝突港の当局者によると、タンカーは、ミシシッピ川沿いのニューオーリンズ港に停泊していたリバークルーズ船に衝突した。クルーズ船には130人以上が乗っていたという。モレノ市長は記者会見で、タンカーの「アトランティック・アスファルト」が「制御を失い」、米アメリカンクルーズラインのリバークルーズ船に衝突したと説明した。港の複数の当局者によると、事故が起きたのは午後0時半ごろ。市長によると、32人が地元の病院で治療を受けているが、命に関わるけがを負った人はいない。

title: マイクロソフト 大規模障害を謝罪
body: 【AFP＝時事】米マイクロソフトは13日、世界各地の公共サービスや企業に支障を及ぼした大規模障害について謝罪した。メールサービス「アウトルック」などが「広範に復旧した」と述べ、全面復旧に向けた作業を続けている。【写真】インドのマイクロソフト事務所前を飛ぶハト同社は、複数のマイクロソフト製品に影響し、医療サービスの混乱や企業の決算発表の遅延、学校での連絡業務への支障を引き起こした今回の障害について、サイバー攻撃などが原因ではないとしている。マイクロソフトはX（旧ツイッター）に「今回の障害がお客様や関係各社に引き起こした混乱を深くおわびする」と投稿した。さらに「当社のサービス全体で広範な復旧と安定化が見られている。これはサイバーやAIエージェントとは関係のない技術的な問題だ」と説明した。障害情報サイト「ダウンディテクター」によると、今回の障害により74の国と地域でマイクロソフト製品が利用できなくなり、米大陸のほか、欧州、アジア、アフリカの一部で利用者に影響が出た。英国の主要労働組合は、障害が同国の医療サービスに「深刻な影響」を与えたと指摘した。インドの航空各社は、顧客からの問い合わせが届いていない可能性があると警告し、ニュージーランド移民局は、障害のためすべてのビザ申請の処理を停止せざるを得なくなったと明らかにした。赤沢亮正経済産業相は、マイクロソフト製品が「非常に多くの人」に利用されているとして、障害が「重大な影響」を及ぼすと警告した。マイクロソフトは12日、障害の原因についてインフラへの「負荷増大」だと述べ、13日には「以前のネットワーク容量増強時に生じた問題が、最近のネットワーク変更を受けて表面化したことによるものだ」と説明した。その上で「根本的な問題には対処しており、残る顧客と地域へのサービス復旧を引き続き進めている」とした。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 婚活に300万円課金 結婚した男性
body:
「30歳になるころには結婚しているものだと思っていました」。そう振り返るのは、静岡県在住のヨシオさん（47歳）だ。⇒【写真】大学時代のヨシオさん。一浪の末、名古屋大学に進学したヨシオさんは36歳で婚活を始めたものの、パーティーに通っても、結婚相談所に入っても、なかなか進展がない。ようやく進んだ真剣交際も、結婚後の生活をめぐる考えの違いから破談になる始末。ヨシオさんは学生時代以来彼女はおらず、婚活当時の年収は350万円ほど。それでも出会いを求め続け、3年の月日と300万円ほどを婚活に費やし、40歳で7歳年下の女性と結婚できた。決して恵まれた条件ではないなか、結婚をつかみ取ったアラフォー男性の婚活に迫る。
婚活を始めたのは、地元静岡の実家に戻り、再就職した直後だった。「それまでは名古屋でしばらく定職にもつかない暮らしをしていましたが、結婚したいならそろそろ動かないと、と思って静岡に帰りました。でも、社会人になってから女性と付き合った経験はなく、自分から積極的に行ける性格でもなかった。女性と話すと緊張して、汗をかいたり、体が熱くなったりすることもありました」ヨシオさんがまず足を運んだのが婚活パーティー。最初の1年半は、ここで出会いを探した。「多いときは毎週土日の昼と夜に参加することもザラ。午前中に会った人に、午後の別のパーティーで『また会いましたね』と再会することもありました（笑）。毎週2、3回行っていたと考えると、1年半で180回くらいは参加したんじゃないでしょうか。参加費は4000～7000円ほど。交通費もかかるので、かなりの出費でしたね」
しかし、結婚までの道のりは遠いままだった。「連絡先交換ができる『マッチング』になかなかたどり着けず、最初は3回に1回だったのが、5回に1回になったり、10回続けてダメだったり。プロフィールカードの書き方を工夫したり、話すネタを用意するようになってもなかなかうまくいきませんでした」連絡先を交換してデートに進んでも、スタート地点に立っただけ。異性との交際経験に乏しいヨシオさんには、“ただの会話”さえハードルが高かった。「デートで行くような場所を知らなくて、『ここ、いいですよね』と言われても、『そうなんですか。行ったことがないので』となってしまう。話がそこで終わって全然盛り上がらないんです。店を提案しても、定休日で別の場所を探し直しているうちに、連絡が途切れてしまうこともありました」明らかに失敗したとわかれば、次は同じことをしないようにできます。でも、何も連絡がないまま終わることも多くて。どこがダメだったのかわからないんですよね」

title: 全米 航空機の地上待機命令を解除
body: アメリカの連邦航空局はさきほど、大規模な通信障害を理由に全米の空港を対象に出していた航空機の地上待機命令を解除しました。

title: 米中露首脳会談 19日に中国で開催
body: 米ホワイトハウスは13日、トランプ大統領が中国の習近平（シーチンピン）国家主席、ロシアのプーチン大統領と19日に中国の深圳で会談すると明らかにした。米中ロ3カ国による正式な首脳会談は史上初めてとみられる。【画像】「終わりの始まり」トランプ外交　中ロ朝の指導者に操られるリスクトランプ氏は深圳で18、19両日に開かれるアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に参加する予定で、それに合わせて3カ国会談を行うとの見通しを示していた。プーチン氏も当初から前向きな姿勢を見せていた。会談での議題について、トランプ氏はこれまで核軍備管理などに言及している。ホワイトハウス高官は13日、「大統領は核兵器の拡散が極めて危険だと考えている」と説明し、世界で最も多くの核兵器を持つ3カ国首脳による最初の対話だと強調した。一方、今回の会談では「いかなる合意に至ることも予想していない」と述べ、核軍縮に向けた「出発点」と位置づけた。

title: 米NYでビル崩壊 瞬間の内部映像
body: 11日、アメリカ・ニューヨークのブルックリンで3階建ての建物が崩落した事故。巻き込まれた隣の建物は、外壁がはがれ落ちて部屋がむき出しに。この階段の前に設置されたカメラが崩落の瞬間を捉えていました。大きな音を立てながら、壁が一気に崩れ落ちます。砂ぼこりが舞い上がり、騒然とする現場。その後、消防隊員の呼びかけで部屋の中から人が出てきますが、壁がなくなったまさかの状況に思わず後ずさり。隊員の手を握り、1歩1歩慎重に階段を降りていきます。市当局によりますと、これまでに2人の子どもを含む8人が死亡、18人がけがをしたということです。

title: イラン側 バーレーンの米施設攻撃
body: ［１３日　ロイター］ - イランのイスラム‌革命防衛隊は１３日、⁠バーレーンにある米軍の早​期警戒レーダーを標的‌に攻撃を実施したと発‌表した。‌イラン国​営メディアが伝え‌た。湾岸諸国にあ‌る米軍施​設に対する攻‌撃の発表は、９月上旬⁠以来となる。革命防衛隊は、イラン⁠南部ホル​モズ‌ガン州シリクの通信塔に対する「⁠敵によ⁠る空爆」への報復だと⁠した。米国およびバー‌レー⁠ンのコメント​は得られていない。

title: バンス氏 米大統領選見送り検討か
body:
【ワシントン共同】米CNNテレビは13日、2028年大統領選の共和党候補選びを巡り、有力候補と目されるバンス副大統領（42）が出馬見送りを検討していると伝えた。対イラン軍事作戦に伴う物価高が影響して3日の中間選挙で共和党が惨敗したことを受け、党を再建できるかどうか疑念を抱いている。バンス氏に近い関係者らの話としている。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
共和党の候補者争いを巡っては、南部フロリダ州のデサンティス知事やクルーズ上院議員らが出馬の可能性をうかがっているとされる。トランプ大統領の後継候補選びは混沌としてきた。中間選挙では「MAGA（米国を再び偉大に）」派の間で亀裂が入り、24年大統領選でトランプ氏を支持した白人や中南米系（ヒスパニック）らが離反。共和党は強固な地盤としてきた州や選挙区で相次いで敗北し、大統領選に向けて危機感を強めている。CNNによると、バンス氏はMAGA派を中心とした支持層からの信頼回復に自身が先頭に立つべきかどうか迷っている。

title: タマホーム 保険代理業を廃業へ
body: 住宅メーカーのタマホームの社員が火災保険の保険金の不正請求をしていた問題で、同社は14日、保険代理業の廃業に向けて、損害保険会社に申し入れをしたと発表した。これまでの社内調査と並行して、外部の専門家も交えた調査を検討していることも明らかにした。【写真】タマホーム本社=2026年11月11日午前11時25分、東京都港区高輪3丁目、小川聡仁撮影同社は注文住宅を建てた客などに対し、損保の保険商品を販売する保険代理業を担ってきた。既存の客は、別の保険代理店に移管する予定だといい、同社は「お客さま及び関係者の皆様からの信頼回復に向けた対応の一環」としている。新たに検討している調査は第三者委員会ではなく、社内調査だという。タマホームを巡っては、高松支店（香川県）の複数の社員が、同じ写真の使い回しによる保険金の架空請求や水増し請求を少なくとも数百件していたことが判明している。不正請求を受けて、損害保険ジャパンと三井住友海上火災保険がタマホームに対し、火災保険の新規販売を停止させる方針を示し、同じく不正請求を受けた東京海上日動火災保険も、販売を停止させる方向で検討している。タマホーム1998年に設立。2002年に保険代理業の登録をしていた。（小川聡仁）

title: 3メガバンク中間決算 最高益更新
body:
三菱ＵＦＪなど３メガバンクグループは１３日、２０２６年９月中間連結決算を発表した。金利上昇や企業の旺盛な資金需要を背景に最終利益はそろって最高を更新し、３メガ合計で前年同期比２１・１％増の３兆５３０５億円と好調だ。ただ先行きは、個人向け国債への預金流出やＡＩ（人工知能）を巡る規制強化への懸念もあり、不透明感も漂う。（長原和磨、岡田実優）【写真】三菱ＵＦＪのデジタル新銀行、キャッシュカード発行せず
「目標は意欲的に設定したが、しっかり成果を出せた。順調に推移している」
三菱ＵＦＪフィナンシャル・グループ（ＦＧ）の半沢淳一社長は１３日、東京都内で開いた決算記者会見で手応えを語った。
３グループの最終利益はそろって過去最高だった。三菱ＵＦＪＦＧが前年同期比２６・１％増の１兆６３０８億円、三井住友ＦＧが７・５％増の１兆３１億円、みずほＦＧが２９・９％増の８９６４億円。三井住友は半期として初めて１兆円を超えた。
２７年３月期の最終利益見通しもそろって引き上げ、３メガ合計で６・３兆円を見込む。
業績拡大をけん引したのは国内金利の上昇だ。日銀が利上げを進めたことで、銀行が企業などに貸し出す際の金利が上昇し、預金金利との差で得られる「利ざや」が拡大した。
企業の資金需要も追い風となる。ＡＩ関連や半導体分野などで資金調達の動きが広がり、３メガ傘下行の２６年９月時点の国内貸出残高は前年同期比３～１０％程度増加した。三井住友ＦＧの中島達社長は「法人顧客の資金需要は引き続き旺盛だった」と振り返った。
預入金利の上昇に伴い、貸し出し原資となる預金も３グループで伸びた。集めた預金を貸し出しに回し、利益を得る好循環が生まれている。
米中間選挙で民主党が大勝し、データセンター建設やＡＩ開発への規制が強まるとの懸念から、ハイテク関連投資が鈍るとの観測が出ている。米半導体大手エヌビディアの経営を巡る混乱も収束が見通せず、関連産業の投資意欲に冷や水を浴びせる可能性がある。

title: FRB 市場の最大脅威は「AI関連」
body: 【ワシントン共同】米連邦準備制度理事会（FRB）が13日公表した金融安定報告書で、市場関係者が人工知能（AI）を使ったサイバー攻撃を含めたAI関連の問題を金融安定にとっての最大の脅威と受け止めていることが分かった。5月公表の前回報告書と比べ、長期金利の動向への警戒感も強まった。FRBは米国の金融の安定性を巡る短期的な懸念を市場関係者に聞き取り、半年に1度、報告書を公表している。今回の調査は9、10月に実施した。AI関連を脅威に挙げた人の割合は、前回の50％から87％に拡大した。回答者はサイバー攻撃に加え、上昇傾向のAI関連銘柄で、業績が想定を下回った場合の株価急落の可能性などを挙げた。

title: 「週明け怖い」MS障害の影響広く
body: 米IT大手マイクロソフト（MS）のメールや業務ソフトなどで起きた世界的なシステム障害は、国内でも影響が広がった。「仕事にならない」「週明けが怖い」。多くの業界で連絡手段を電話に切り替えるなどして対応に追われた。【写真で見る】2年前には…WindowsPCで大規模な不具合コンサルティング会社に勤める50代男性は、メールソフト「アウトルック」などを使っている。取引先とはメールでの連絡を基本としているが、障害でこれまでの履歴も確認できず、書類もやりとりできない。この日は電話で不具合の状況を取引先と共有し、1日が終わったという。男性は「メールが復旧すれば、きょうのやりとりをまた残さなければならず、手間がかかる。早く復旧してほしい」と訴えた。障害はさまざまな業界に及んだ。仙台国際ホテル（仙台市）では、宿泊やクリスマスケーキなどの予約状況の確認、通知にアウトルックを利用しているが、電話で予約するよう呼びかけた。社内での連絡手段も紙ベースに変えたという。担当者は「障害が長期化すれば、現場の負担増加は避けられない」と話す。佐川急便では、手荷物の一時預かりサービスのウェブ予約ができなくなった。東京都港区では業務効率化で導入した生成AI（人工知能）「コパイロット」が使えず、職員らの資料作成に影響が出たという。教育現場からも困惑の声が上がった。東京農業大（東京都世田谷区）ではクラウドサービス「ワンドライブ」を使っており、授業教材を一時ダウンロードできなくなった。メールの送受信もできず、広報担当者は「大学に寄せられるメールはただでさえ、週末にたまってしまう。週明けが怖い」と嘆いた。東京都府中市の市立中学校では授業が止まることはなかったが、教育委員会とのやりとりや部活動の大会参加申し込みなどについて、電話とファクスでの連絡に切り替えたという。校長は「外部とのやりとりができず、仕事にならない。生徒への影響が出ないうちに何とか復旧してほしい」と話した。【古瀬弘治、倉沢仁志、尾上雅典、斎藤文太郎】

title: 「人生初FAX」MS障害で代替手段
body:
米マイクロソフトのメールサービス「アウトルック」などで日本時間の１３日未明に明らかになった大規模なシステム障害は、多くの企業や官公庁、大学などに影響を与えた。慣れ親しんだサービスが突如として使えなくなる事態となり、多くの利用者が代替手段での対応を余儀なくされた。【写真】大規模障害を謝罪「重く受け止めている」…全面復旧見通し立たず
「メールもＡＩ（人工知能）も使えず、仕事に時間がかかって大変だった」
フリーランスで司会業などの仕事を請け負う関西地方在住の２０歳代女性は、ため息を漏らした。女性は普段、アウトルックのメールで取引先に資料を送付しているが、この日は自宅最寄りのコンビニ店からファクスで送った。仕事に多用する生成ＡＩサービス「コパイロット」も使えず、作業に長時間を要したといい、「ＡＩにかなり頼っているので苦労した。早く復旧してほしい」と語った。
都内の商社に勤める会社員男性（２５）は、勤務先で取引先との連絡をメールからファクスに急きょ切り替え、発注内容や見積もりをファクスで送り続けた。男性は「人生で初めてファクスを使ったが、送信後に電話で受信を確認しなければならず、本当に疲れた」と振り返り、「メールの便利さを実感したが、一つのサービスに頼るのは危ないと感じた」と話した。
企業への影響も広がった。ビックカメラは１３日、インターネット経由の取り置きサービスや各店舗での接客予約サービスが利用できない状態となったほか、ネット通販の問い合わせ窓口へのメール対応にも遅れが生じた。
佐川急便でも、手荷物の預かりサービスの事前予約ができなくなった。駅や観光地などにある店舗で荷物を預かるサービスだが、予約完了メールを送信できないため、予約受け付けを見合わせたという。

title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
summary: The collision leaves 32 people in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for.
body:
Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New Orleans
Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.
The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".
The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".
"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.
Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.
Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.
Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.
Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what happened.
Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he saw the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.
"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."
Holford added that he saw passengers and crew members "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.
The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.
Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.

title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
summary: Experts say the event is a "stark reminder" of how heavily the world relies on a small group of big tech providers.
body:
Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.
Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.
By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, andtrains, hospitals and courts in North America.
Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.
Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill

title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
summary: Microsoft says it is continuing to restore services including Outlook and Teams following a global outage.
body:
Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage
A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world.
Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced.
Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue
Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.
From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.
"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.
Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".
In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.
Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".
The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.
When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.
Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies,disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK,GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.

title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
summary: Elon Musk’s company aborted an attempted catch of the rocket’s booster - instead it came down in the ocean.
body:
The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean as it burst into flames
SpaceX aborted its attempt to catch the bottom part of its huge Starship rocket during its latest test flight.
The aim was to catch it using the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on the launch tower as it returned to Earth, but instead it was diverted to  the ocean, bursting into flames as it came  down.
The top part of the rocket is now continuing its journey to space, and SpaceX will decide whether it will try to catch this rocket stage - at about 1515 local time (2115 GMT) on Saturday.
It's the company's first attempt to fully recover its rocket, paving the way for making Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.
Starship is the tallest and most powerful rocket ever built
The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) on Friday.
It was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned to the launch tower, but instead it was diverted to the ocean.
During a stream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority, and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely."
The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet from space.
The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.
In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than a hundred times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.
But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, President of Royal Aeronautical Society.
"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.
"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."
What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?
Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.
But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do.  The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.
Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
summary: Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself.
body:
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?
The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.
Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.
Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.
But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.
Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.
The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.
US intelligence reportedlysuspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.
On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.
This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.
Now the political pressure is building.
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to block Megaspeed
Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.
Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.
There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.
The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.
Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?
Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?

title: Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
summary: Scott Bessent told CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
body:
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.
Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.
Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," hetold CNBC's Squawk Box programme,external.
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.
In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media.
How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
Huang has beensummoned to testifybefore the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.
Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.
A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
summary: Experts warn that using AI to enhance property images can go too far and mislead prospective buyers.
body:
The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r)
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?
Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.
From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.
But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".
So how much AI enhancement is too much?
Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.
But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.
"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."
For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.
AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious
It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.
But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.
"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."
All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.
Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.
It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.
According to a recent survey,externalof 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.
Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.
He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.
But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.
"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."
He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.
Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left
Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.
In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.
In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.
Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.
"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.
In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug
A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".
"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."
Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.
But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.
Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.
He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.
"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
summary: Reform's Zia Yusuf and Tory Chris Philp were speaking against converting a former military site into asylum accommodation.
body:
Watch: Philp and Yusuf have public clash over immigration
Conservative MP Chris Philp and Reform UK's Zia Yusuf had a blazing row at a joint press conference, as they joined villagers protesting against asylum accommodation plans.
The pair clashed when sharing a platform in Piddington to oppose converting a former military site at MoD Bicester into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.
The two politicians were invited to make speeches about the plans, but things became heated after Yusuf asked Philp to apologise for the Conservatives' record on immigration.
Philp, the shadow home secretary, told Yusuf to "calm down" and accused him of "cheap politics", an assertion Reform's home affairs spokesman dismissed.
Asylum centre on military base near Piddington approved
A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.
The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.
There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.
In September,Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UKover the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.
Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.
Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.
Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.
He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.
"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"
Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.
He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".
Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."
Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.
Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."
Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.
As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."
Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".
McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."
While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.
Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party asreplacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she wouldrather have another general electionthan do a deal with Reform to secure power.
Up to 1,256 men could be housed at the site near Bicester under the plans
Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels.
Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it shouldnot just be the poorest communitiesreceiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.
Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.
Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".
He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

title: Firm offers to fake artworks for wealthy migrants seeking UK 'talent' visas - BBC investigation
summary: Going undercover to expose an elaborate fraud aimed at obtaining fast-track settlement for wealthy migrants.
body:
Watch: BBC undercover reporter is offered fake art and awards for 'talent' visa
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.
The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.
Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.
Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.
We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.
A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.
No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.
In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.
A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.
"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.
Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written
Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.
The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.
A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".
They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".
The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.
Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.
Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media
During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:
At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying
The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application
For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application
iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.
We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath ofour first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.
The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.
A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.
In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."
An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries
In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".
Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.
While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".
The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.
Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.
About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.
Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.
The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.
Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".
We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent
Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.
"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.
Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.
Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.
To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.
During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.
Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award
Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.
The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.
It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.
Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.
This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.
Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.
The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.
The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.
The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal
During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.
The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.
"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."
He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".
When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.
"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.
iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporte

title: Tories pay artist for Burnham images after legal threat
summary: Stanley Chow had threatened to sue the Conservative Party for using his illustrations of the PM.
body:
The Conservatives handed out bottles with Chow's illustration on them at their party conference
The Conservatives have agreed to pay an artist who threatened to sue the party after it used his illustration of Andy Burnham to mock the prime minister.
Stanley Chow posted on Facebook that the party had used the picture - which Burnham has used on social media - without permission.
He had sought legal advice and threatened to take action against the party. It is understood the Tories agreed to pay a £1,000 fee for use of the image - and contributed an unknown sum to Chow's legal fees.
The Conservatives had distributed water bottles with the image on them - accusing Burnham of being a "bottler".
Chow posted on Facebook: "The Conservative Party have settled after their recent indiscretion of using my image without my permission."
He added: "Maybe ask first… admittedly I would have said no, but it would have been a damn sight cheaper for the Tory Party if they just hired any illustrator to do their take on a cartoon of Burnham… hopefully this a lesson learned. Copyright matters."
A Conservative spokesman said: "The Conservative Party values the importance of intellectual property in the creative industries. We consider this matter closed."
The original image of Andy Burnham was created by Chow in 2021
Manchester United fan Chow, a Labour supporter, has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho.
He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city.
He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager.

title: Labour lost its connection with voters, says Welsh leader
summary: On Saturday, Labour will publish a review into its historic election defeat in May’s Senedd election.
body:
Ken Skates took over as leader of Welsh Labour after the May defeat
Labour lost its connection with previously loyal voters at May's Senedd election, the party's leader has said.
Officials will publish on Saturday a review of Labour's historic election defeat in the May Senedd election.
Speaking to BBC Wales, Ken Skates said it was "absolutely obvious" that the party needed to rediscover its purpose and reconnect with people the "length and breadth of Wales".
Labour was thrown out of power at the election when it was reduced from 30 seats in the Welsh Parliament to nine.
It is holding its first party conference since Labour went into opposition, and Plaid Cymru took over the Welsh government.
After years of trailing Labour, Plaid won the largest number of seats, allowing party leader Rhun ap Iorwerth to become first minister.
Labour had led the Welsh government since devolution began 27 years ago.
Skates, who took over as leader following the election, said: "According to the review, it's absolutely obvious that we needed to rediscover our purpose".
He said the party needed to "strengthen" its "soul" and "reestablish that powerful contract between us as a movement in Welsh Labour and the people of Wales who share our values".
He said he could not disclose what the review, by Professor Anand Menon of King's College London, will say the day before conference.
"But I can say this - that people still believe that we share the fundamental values that they have and that they hold dear."
Ken Skates will address the party's conference in Llandudno on Friday
Asked what he stood for as leader, Skates said: "My passion has always been quite fundamental that no young person should be left behind because of disadvantage when growing up, that every person in life should have the best opportunity to succeed."
He said he and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "share a huge number of similarities".
"Catholic influences, strong community influence, we support the same football team, [we] went to the same university, we both enjoy running."
"I was determined to ensure that this review is dispassionate, independent and objective," he said.
"We don't have a version of the truth, we have the objective truth. And I would hope that no matter how tough it is, people will accept the findings and will be part of the movement that will build again."
The conference is taking place in Venue Cymru
Since becoming prime minister, Burnham haslobbied the Welsh government to devolve more powers to Wales' regions.
The policy has been criticised by some former Welsh ministers. Lee Waters, former transport minister, said it"just doesn't work"in a Welsh context.
The Plaid Welsh government has promised a green paper looking at the powers of councils, with legislation possibly after the next election in 2030.
Skates said people in Wales were telling the party they wanted more powers for their communities.
"We want more powers to come to the Senedd, to Cardiff Bay, but we also want more powers out of Cardiff Bay in our communities," he said. "That's what people want."
He said the review would make clear "about what people in Wales want most, which is more power in their communities."
Skates is expected to address the conference on Saturday.

title: Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
summary: Any revolt among MPs is likely to be smaller than the one that badly damaged Keir Starmer's government.
body:
A review by Alan Milburn (left) could create political headaches for Andy Burnham
Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.
He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street.
Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms.
To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out.
Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government.
Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks.
Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).
In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit.
Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorus to water.
But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected.
Importantly, two of the most effective organisers of last year's welfare rebellion are batting for the current prime minister, rather than against the previous one.
Louise Haigh is now the most powerful cabinet minister after Andy Burnham himself, while Anneliese Midgeley is his chief whip.
And the MP who fronted that rebellion - Meg Hillier - has said she wants to give Milburn's proposals a "fair wind".
There are also clear differences to the previous approach to welfare reform.
First, it is not being presented as primarily a cost-cutting exercise with pre-determined savings.
Instead, there will be upfront investment to provide more support to unemployed young people, and a timeframe for net savings likely to be set at around a decade – gradualism, not a short, sharp shock.
Second, last year's initial reforms would have affected people in all age groups, whilst benefit cuts this time would be limited to the under 25s, who make up around 11% of Pip claimants.

I've spoken to government ministers who had expressed concerns – at least privately – about the changes devised previously by Rachel Reeves and Liz Kendall.  This time, they are on board.
One of them told me that so long as there was enough support for young people, with guaranteed jobs and training, MPs would be "fine" with some benefit cuts.
But they added that it was vital that those who really couldn't work wouldn't be worse off.
Milburn will suggest there could even be enhanced payments for people in this category, while some young people with disabilities who lose out on Pip could nonetheless be given an additional "allowance" to help with living costs.
Another minister who opposed the previous reforms praised the process this time.
There had been a high level of engagement not just from Milburn, but Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms.
One minister was a little more cautious, suggesting support for a reduction in benefits would depend on what the entire "package" of reforms looked like.
Milburn's recommendations are likely to be wide-ranging – from pre-school policies to how the NHS deals with mental health.
Some of the eventual 49 rebels from last year are in a similar place.
York MP Rachael Maskell told me it was essential that she saw the detail of the proposals rather than the "drip, drip" of press reports which would "cause young people stress and distress".
She felt withdrawing Pip from young people was "like a sledgehammer to crack a nut" and was concerned that some disabled people required it to remain in work.
She also suggested that the government "shouldn't just point the finger at young people," and should look closely at how employers could take more youngsters on.
Stroud MP Simon Opher also voted against the government on welfare last year.
He told me there was a "crisis" with so many Neets, and Milburn had come up with a "credible solution".
But he believes cutting benefits should be a "last resort" and is worried about restricting access to the health element of Universal Credit, as a quarter of young claimants aren't Neet. He concludes that the "devil will be in the detail".
So much of politics - like comedy – depends on timing.
For some sceptics, including serving ministers, the Milburn proposals will be more warmly welcomed if support for young people is in place before entitlements are withdrawn.
But for some Labour MPs, cutting payments to existing claimants crosses a line.
Clapham and Brixton Hill MP Bell Ribiero-Addy has she wasn't sure she could back cuts.
Referring to Pip, she didn't believe that "you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work".
And another MP on the left of the party, Brian Leishman, told the BBC he couldn't back benefits cuts as "we are in the middle of a cost of living crisis".
So a welfare rebellion seems guaranteed if Burnham accepts Milburn's recommendations.
But it seems unlikely to be of the same scale, or have a similar level of political jeopardy to the one which shook the Starmer government.
